Chapter Seven: Microaggressions and the Unseen Labor of Survival.
There’s a kind of work that rarely gets noticed—a steady, almost invisible effort that goes into getting through a world that’s not always kind or welcoming. You won’t find this work on a resume, and it doesn’t show up in a paycheck. But you can feel its weight. It’s the work of always being ready—anticipating a comment, preparing an explanation, deciding if this is the moment to speak up, or if it’s safer to let it slide.
Imagine you’re on your morning commute. The train is packed, and you can sense the tension creeping into your shoulders. Someone’s stare lingers just a little too long. There’s an empty seat, but no one takes it, even as the car gets more crowded. And you can’t help but wonder— is it something about me? That question—quiet but persistent—never really goes away, does it?
Then, at work, it continues. Maybe a colleague cracks a joke that just doesn’t sit right. Laughter circles the room, and you find yourself smiling along, even though your stomach tightens. Later, maybe in the bathroom, you replay what happened and ask yourself, “Should I have said something?” There’s always this mental math—will speaking up help, or will it just make things harder?
And it’s not just at work. It follows you into stores, onto sidewalks, into classrooms. There’s this ongoing need to manage how others see you, to always be a little bit on guard, ready to defend your place. Most people don’t notice this constant vigilance, but for those who live it, the cost is real. It can show up as exhaustion, irritability, or just feeling stretched so thin you might snap.
Sometimes, though, this unseen labor is shared. Friends get together and trade stories—comparing notes on the day’s microaggressions. There’s comfort in knowing someone else gets it, but also this frustration: why should we have to do this work at all? These conversations are a mix of laughter and sighs—a way to get by, even if they don’t fix the problem.
Over time, all those little moments can pile up. Your body absorbs the stress, and your mind gets tired. Still, most people keep going—finding small ways to recharge. Maybe it’s a walk outside, playing your favorite song, or just a quiet night at home. These little rituals become acts of self-preservation.
The hope is that by naming this invisible labor, we can start to change it. Maybe, just maybe, people who never noticed before will begin to see it—and the weight can be shared a little more fairly. But until that day comes, the work continues. Quiet, invisible, and absolutely essential.
